transcript:
Meeting header: 
Date: 2026-12-20 17:00 UTC
Duration: ~57 minutes
Attendees: Ethan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Carlos (Redwood), Samir (Ascend), Juno (Ascend SRE), Lena (Ascend Data Eng)

Auto-summary: intermittent p99 spikes tied to short-lived 'microbursts' during high concurrency; hypothesis: KV cache hotspotting + extra network hop via VPC NAT gateway under burst; experiment plan: run 1000 short-window requests with both streaming on and off, compare p95/p99, capture full traces.

-- Transcript (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect) --
00:00 Ethan: okay, hey everyone thanks for doing this late call. I think Samir said this was an emergency-ish microburst. can you give a quick recap?
00:12 Samir: yeah thanks, uh so over the last two weeks we've been seeing these sudden p99 jumps, they last like 10 to 30 seconds and then drop back. p95 is fine most of the time so it's really the tail. We pushed a bunch of changes to our prompt routing at the same time so it's hard to tell if it's client side or on the runtime.
00:30 Juno: the SRE side we've ruled out app GC, we clocked the upstream latency to the Redwood endpoint and saw small spikes but some traces show an extra 40-60ms sometimes. worth noting our prod cluster is in a VPC that peers to Redwood via a transit VPC and uses NAT in one az for egress.
00:51 Maya: thanks, that's super helpful. a quick framing: microbursts (short high qps bursts) can expose KV cache hotkeying (one shard getting heavy), queueing in the batcher, or network amplification if there's an unexpected hop. we usually split the investigation across three axes: runtime (batcher, kv), networking (hops, ENI, nat), and model exec (quantization and kernel selection).
01:14 Lena: can you explain the KV cache hotkey thing again? we call it 'prefix cache' in house so names differ.
01:22 Maya: sure. imagine many requests sharing a common prefix or prompt that touches the same KV entries; that shard gets a lot of concurrent reads/writes, so one GPU/node becomes a hotspot. continuous batching can compound that because many requests are queued for the same node, increasing p99 even if average stays low. we sometimes see it when customers have personalization tokens or static system prompts.
01:46 Samir: our telemetry shows a handful of prompt templates get 60% of the requests during promos. so plausible.
01:54 Ethan: question — Ascend is on a VPC peering topology with a transit setup; Juno mentioned NAT in one AZ. NAT can add serialization or queueing if it's an instance-based NAT or uses small connection pools, so that could explain intermittent extra hops and queuing. any recent change to that?
02:09 Juno: we did increase our outbound flow logging and there's a flapping ENI event last week but thought it was transient. worth investigating.
02:17 Maya: good, combine that with a microburst and you can see p99 blow up. for experiments, we want to: 1) reproduce microbursts with a synthetic runner that precisely controls short-high qps windows, 2) run with streaming enabled (token-by-token) and streaming disabled (full response) to see serialization differences, 3) log per-hop millisecond timings including TLS handshake, and 4) capture KV cache hit distribution across shards.
02:45 Carlos: also we'll toggle quantization profiles — 8-bit vs 4-bit — because sometimes 4-bit inference can increase variance slightly if kernels are less mature on the GPU, which shows up at the tail.
03:00 Lena: that surprised me; I'd thought quant is monotonic for latency.
03:05 Maya: normally yes for average, but tail depends on micro-ops support on the card and kernel fallback behavior. if an op falls back to slower path for certain token lengths or attention patterns you can see a handful of requests take 2-3x longer.
03:24 Samir: okay. in terms of scope, we care about strict p99 SLO of 350ms for customer-facing chat. p95 under 100ms is great but p99 is killing us.
03:36 Ethan: thanks. quick note — dedicated capacity vs hosted: dedicated gives you cleaner isolation and you can pin model variants and scaling differently; hosted has more routing layers but we also have smarter routing and fallbacks. For microbursts dedicated can help if the problem is noisy neighbors, but if it's your VPC topology the difference is smaller.
03:57 Juno: we'd prefer hosted initially because we don't want to manage infra, but if we can't get p99 under control that becomes a procurement discussion.
04:06 Maya: fair. let's walk through the instrumentation points. we'll need: per-request traces with tags for prefix id, kv-shard-id, model variant, whether streaming enabled, and TLS connect times. Ascend: can you add a unique request-id header? that helps correlate logs.
04:25 Samir: yes we can. we'll add X-Ascend-Req to the next deploy.
04:29 Maya: great. Also, we'll instrument the runtime's batcher metrics: queue length distribution, batch sizes, and per-batch exec time. in Redwood runtime we expose continuous batching metrics but sometimes customers run an aggressive batch window. if the batch window spikes during microbursts you can get longer tail.
04:52 Lena: is continuous batching enabled by default? does it differ for streaming?
04:58 Maya: continuous batching is enabled; streaming adds complexity because token streaming has lower per-token latency but higher sensitivity to small delays (additional scheduling overhead). non-streaming (we call it full-response) tends to group into larger batches more often so p95 improves but p99 can get worse if small requests wait behind big ones. streaming sometimes hides tail by emitting early tokens, but if the initial tokens are delayed that's visible to the user.
05:31 Juno: interesting, so there's a tradeoff. what about the kernel selection and quantization interplay?
05:38 Maya: kernels get selected by model shape, sequence length, and quant profile. 4-bit paths can be faster but are more likely to hit less-tested kernels on some GPUs. that shows up as higher variance. a mitigation is to pin a quant profile on critical routes or run a secondary fallback to 8-bit for requests that cross a certain prefix length threshold.
06:00 Samir: how do you detect that during runtime? automatic?
06:04 Maya: we have heuristics and telemetry. e.g., track per-model exec time histogram by quant profile and rollback if p99 increases after rollout. Redwood Optimize also suggests quant settings per workload.
06:17 Ethan: okay, let's move to networking. Juno, can you share the VPC path? we want to identify possible extra hops (Transit VPC, NAT, firewall appliance).
06:26 Juno: yes I can share a diagram after. we have a transit VPC in us-east-1, peering to Redwood in the same region; egress goes through a managed NAT gateway for that AZ and there are some proxy appliances for security scanning.
06:40 Maya: proxies and security appliances can add extra TLS termination or multiplexing overhead. also keep an eye on ephemeral port exhaustion under burst which can queue connections. For long-lived connections we recommend gRPC/keepalive where possible to reduce TLS handshake spikes.
06:56 Lena: we use HTTP/1.1 with short connections today. perhaps switching to HTTP/2 or gRPC would help?
07:03 Maya: typically yes. gRPC with keepalive reduces per-request handshake cost and smooths microburst impacts. But that requires client changes.
07:10 Carlos: also, if the transit path has intermittent ENI flaps, the cluster may route traffic via a different AZ adding 30-50ms; that would explain some traces.
07:21 Samir: we saw those AZ jumps in cloudwatch last week.
07:25 Maya: okay. proposed experiments (we'll log results in a shared sheet):
- Synthetic microburst runner: short windows 100-200RPS, durations 5s/15s/30s, payload sizes matching prod (avg tokens), both streaming on/off.
- KV cache heatmap: run same prefix heavy vs uniform traffic to see shard imbalance.
- Network path variant test: run from client in same subnet vs across transit VS via a bastion to mimic a different path.
- Quant profiles: run identical requests with 4-bit vs 8-bit to compare p95/p99 distributions.

08:05 Juno: how do we capture per-hop timing? VPC flow logs are coarse.
08:11 Maya: we'll instrument client and runtime to emit timestamps for: client send, TCP connect end, TLS handshake end, request reach runtime (ingress), batch queue enter/exit, model exec start/end, response write start. correlate by request-id. that will show where the 40-60ms is happening.
08:28 Samir: is instrumenting runtime simple? will we need a special build?
08:32 Maya: no, we can enable extended tracing on your Redwood tenant. it's a toggle and will stream structured traces to the bucket you give us. we'll need an S3 bucket or equivalent with write credentials.
08:41 Samir: okay we'll provision a temp bucket and send creds by email.
08:46 Maya: perfect. another point — KV cache eviction behavior on short bursts: if your working set exceeds cache capacity occasionally the cold-cache miss rate spikes and remote fetches cost extra. do you have cache sizing metrics?
08:59 Lena: we only export hit ratio per model, not per-shard.
09:04 Maya: per-shard matters. a 95% overall hit ratio can mask a hot shard at 30% if others are 99%. we'll ask Redwood runtime to add per-shard hit histograms for the test.
09:16 Carlos: also consider prefix aggregation and pre-warming for known heavy prompts during promos — push those prefixes into cache proactively.
09:25 Samir: we could do that. the promo list is known 24hrs ahead usually.
09:29 Maya: cool, that's a good mitigation. regarding batching, we should capture batch size distribution and queue time percentiles. if batcher queue wait gets long during bursts, it's likely the microburst is causing scheduling thrash. You can tune batch window or max batch size to bias towards latency.
09:49 Juno: any quick rules of thumb?
09:52 Maya: if p50<100ms but p99>350ms, try reducing max window to lower queue wait (smaller batches) and enable streaming for chat routes. If that hurts throughput/cost too much, consider dedicated capacity or autoscale with more headroom.
10:10 Samir: how about fallback policies? like fallback to a smaller model or different region under tail spike?
10:15 Ethan: we support automatic fallback routing — e.g., route to cheaper but lower-latency model variants or route to a different region. the tradeoff is output quality. for chat SLOs you might prefer the lower-latency fallback for a short window.
10:28 Lena: can we have per-route fallback thresholds?
10:31 Maya: yes, per-route SLO-based fallbacks. we can set a policy: if p99 > 350ms for >10s then shift 30% traffic to fallback, then escalate.
10:44 Juno: ok good.
10:46 Samir: for instrumentation, what do you need from our side again?
10:49 Maya: request-id header, VPC topology diagram, S3 bucket for traces, and permission to enable extended tracing on your tenant. Also indicate which routes (chat endpoints) to prioritize.
11:02 Samir: we'll get that by Monday.
11:06 Maya: sweet. quick aside on quant: when we run the 4-bit/8-bit comparison, we'll watch kernel fallback logs. if a small percentage of ops are falling back, we'll see long tails. we'll recommend pinning 8-bit for those paths or gating 4-bit behind canary traffic.
11:26 Lena: what's the expected delta between streaming and non-streaming p99?
11:30 Maya: for many customers streaming reduces initial perceived latency but p99 behavior depends. Example: with streaming on you might see p95 20-30ms better, but p99 could be equal or slightly worse if the runtime scheduling has per-token overhead bursts. In tests we saw p99 improvements when token emission starts early even if final completion is later. It's workload dependent.
12:01 Carlos: also note serialization overhead for per-token flushes and network packetization — if NAT or proxy imposes small packet rate limits that can show up.
12:12 Juno: that matches our traces where we see a burst of tiny writes followed by stall.
12:18 Maya: yep. other quick practical mitigations: longer-lived connections, client-side rate-limiting to smooth bursts, pre-warming caches, and a short-lived dedicated pool for promos.
12:33 Samir: promotion windows are predictable so pre-warm is attractive.
12:36 Ethan: let's capture decisions now.
12:38 -- Recap and decisions --
12:39 Maya: (1) Redwood will run synthetic microburst bench with streaming on/off and 4-bit/8-bit variants, record p95/p99, and share raw logs (Maya), (2) Ascend will provide VPC topologies, ENI counts, and enable X-Ascend-Req header (Samir/Juno), (3) both sides will correlate traces in shared S3 bucket and produce an initial root-cause hypothesis within one week.
12:58 Samir: sounds good.
13:01 Ethan: I'll follow up with pricing for a small dedicated pilot and options for pre-warm capacity.
13:07 Lena: thanks all. small nit — can you share documentation pointers for enabling extended tracing and the metrics names?
13:12 Maya: yes I'll send links in the follow-up: runtime trace docs, kv shard metrics, and sample bench script.
13:20 Carlos: note on the bench: we'll attach the runner so you can re-run with different region/peering settings.
13:26 Samir: thanks everyone, appreciate the quick triage.
13:30 Ethan: thanks, we'll send notes and schedule a follow-up check-in for results.

References / Shared artifacts:
- Redwood trace toggle doc (shared): docs.redwood/internal/trace-toggle (link to be shared)
- Bench runner repo: github.com/redwood/bench-microburst (we'll attach)
- VPC diagram (Ascend): will be shared by Samir to the thread

End of call.
